items.title: [Atlas Obscura] Waldkunstpfad in Darmstadt, Germany
items.content_html:
Hidden in the forest on the southern edge of Darmstadt, the Waldkunstpfad turns an ordinary woodland walk into something considerably more surreal. Along the trails, artworks emerge between the trees, lean against trunks, occupy clearings, or use the forest itself as part of the installation. Instead of entering a gallery, visitors simply follow the path and wait to see what the woods have decided to reveal.

The International Forest Art Trail has been running since 2002, with a new theme and a changing group of artists for each edition. Artists from around the world create site-specific works in and around the forest, often using natural or locally appropriate materials. Some pieces are bold and unmistakably artificial; others are so well integrated into their surroundings that they can initially look like something the forest produced on its own.

The result is part sculpture garden, part hiking trail, and part treasure hunt. A fallen branch might turn out to be an artwork. A peculiar wooden structure might suddenly make sense when viewed from the other side. Even familiar landmarks such as the Goethefelsen and Goetheteich become part of the experience.

The trail encourages slow exploration rather than a quick checklist of attractions. There is no grand museum entrance and no velvet rope separating art from nature. The forest is the gallery, the changing seasons are part of the exhibition, and discovering a work around the next bend is half the fun.

Many works remain in the forest beyond the official exhibition period, meaning the trail can continue to evolve between editions. The exact collection therefore depends on when it is visited—a useful excuse to come back and see what has appeared, disappeared, or been reclaimed by the woods.

The main route stretches through the Böllenfalltor forest toward Ludwigshöhe. Bring shoes suitable for woodland paths and keep an eye out: the most interesting artwork may not be the one that announces itself first.

items.title: [Atlas Obscura] Adam’s Gulch  in Ketchum, Idaho
items.content_html:
Mountain bikers and hikers pour into Adam’s Gulch for its 33 miles of interconnected trails, but the gulch has a quieter claim to attention: more than a century ago, it was home to an early ranger station in what became the Ketchum Ranger District.

After the Sawtooth National Forest was established in 1905, its territory was divided into ranger districts, with the first ranger’s station at Adam’s Gulch built in 1909. The district’s administrative center later moved elsewhere, leaving the gulch to become better known for recreation than bureaucracy.

Today, Adam’s Gulch Trailhead is the most popular trailhead in the Ketchum Ranger District. The network begins just outside Ketchum and offers routes ranging from a quick outing on Sunnyside Trail to mountain biking on Forbidden Fruit and longer adventures toward Fox Peak.

The setting helps explain the appeal. Trails thread through the foothills and connect into a much larger network around the Wood River Valley. Wildlife is very much part of that landscape. Idaho Fish and Game has documented both black bears and moose in the Adams Gulch area and has reminded visitors to give wild animals plenty of space.

items.title: [Trip Reports] Sorta highish in the Wind Rivers
items.content_html:
Hey there. Long time, no post.



Just back from a long walkabout in the Winds with my brother. Green River Lakes to Big Sandy via a sorta highish route.



Around 75 miles. Roughly 14,000 feet of vert. Millions of boulders.



About half and half, on-trail versus not.



Skipped Titcomb (didn't want to deal with Knapsack Col) and Cirque of the Towers (socked in with weather), but having visited both previously this wasn't an issue...
